column1: The assistants described in this unit send prompts and code context to {{c1::cloud-based AI models}} for processing.
column2:
A cloud model can receive selected editor context as well as the typed prompt. Check the applicable data policy before including protected material.
Review source

column1: GitHub Copilot context can include code from {{c1::open editor files}}, not just the current line.
column2:
The active line is not the only possible context source. For example, an open settings file can contain values that must stay out of the prompt.
Review source

column1: In data-classification policies, PII stands for {{c1::personally identifiable information}}.
column2:
PII can identify a person, such as a customer record linked to a government identifier. Follow the organization's handling rules before sharing such context.
Review source

column1: A proprietary database design can qualify as a {{c1::trade secret}} even without including table rows.
column2:
A diagram or schema can disclose how a proprietary system works without exposing a single row. Apply the same review to metadata before sharing it.
Review source

column1: Before using cloud AI for regulated SQL data, review the applicable {{c1::compliance requirements}}.
column2:
Identify what data can be shared and which service can process it. Product safeguards are not a substitute for organizational approval.
Review source

column1: GitHub Copilot uses {{c1::content filtering}} to help block harmful or insecure suggestions.
column2:
Filtering can reduce harmful suggestions, but it does not verify each statement. A developer still needs to check the code's behavior and permissions.
Review source

column1: Copilot's public-code matching policy can {{c1::block suggestions}} that match publicly available code.
column2:
This policy checks for matches to public code. It does not establish that the generated SQL is secure or appropriate for the application.
Review source

column1: GitHub Enterprise Cloud organizations can use {{c1::audit logs}} to oversee Copilot-related activity.
column2:
Audit logs support oversight of recorded Copilot events. Check which events are covered before treating the log as a complete account of activity.
Review source

column1: Before sharing a connection string with an AI assistant, replace actual credentials with {{c1::placeholders}}.
column2:
Keep the connection string's structure if it helps explain a problem, but remove live passwords, tokens, and keys. A placeholder has no authentication value.
Review source

column1: The unit recommends {{c1::environment variables}} instead of hardcoded connection secrets in AI-visible files.
column2:
A file can contain the variable name without containing its value. Keep the resolved credential out of editor context and prompts as well.
Review source

column1: Review AI-generated code for accidentally included secrets before {{c1::committing it to source control}}.
column2:
Make sure generated code does not contain usable tokens or passwords. Do not assume a suggestion is free of sensitive values just because an assistant wrote it.
Review source

column1: AI-generated GRANT statements must follow {{c1::least privilege}}, granting only permissions needed for the task.
column2:
Match access to the task. For example, an identity that only inspects metadata does not need permission to update a table.
Review source

column1: For dynamic T-SQL, {{c1::sp_executesql}} supports passing data values separately from the SQL statement text.
column2:
Define parameters in the call and supply their values separately. The procedure name alone does not make input safe if it was embedded in statement text.
Review source

column1: Properly bound SQL parameters treat input as {{c1::literal values}} rather than executable SQL code.
column2:
A bound value stays data rather than changing what the statement means. Parameterization applies to values, not to choosing a table or column name.
Review source

column1: When reviewing an AI-generated SELECT, check for unintended {{c1::data exposure}} to its consumers.
column2:
Think about both fields and rows. A query can return correct results while still revealing information its audience does not need or is not allowed to see.
Review source

column1: The unit recommends a {{c1::dedicated service account}} for an MCP server's database connection.
column2:
Use a distinct identity to scope database access to this integration. Avoid reusing a login with broad privileges just because it can already connect.
Review source

column1: An MCP task that only inspects schema needs access to required {{c1::schema metadata}}, not broad write privileges.
column2:
Schema inspection needs information such as table names and column definitions. It does not require writes or access to the stored values.
Review source

column1: To avoid public-network exposure, an organization can require MCP traffic to use private endpoints or {{c1::VPN connections}}.
column2:
The network path controls where connections can come from. The database still needs to authenticate callers and enforce their permissions.
Review source

column1: MCP {{c1::data sampling}} can expose actual database row values to an AI service.
column2:
A sample can return names or other sensitive values from a row rather than just column definitions. Review what the tool can send before enabling it.
Review source

column1: Copilot in Fabric documents that your data is not used for {{c1::training models}}.
column2:
The training assurance does not prevent the service from processing data to answer a prompt. Check the processing rules separately.
Review source

column1: Encryption {{c1::in transit}} protects AI-service data during network transfer.
column2:
This control protects data moving between the client and the service. It does not decide which data your organization allows you to send.
Review source

column1: Encryption {{c1::at rest}} protects AI-service data in storage.
column2:
This control protects data while it is stored. Use a separate transfer control for data traveling to or from the service.
Review source
